arXiv:2401.09422v1 [cond-mat.str-el] 17 Jan 2024

Where is the spin liquid in maple-leaf quantum magnet?

Pratyay Ghosh Email: pratyay.ghosh@epfl.ch Affiliation: Institute of Physics, Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland
Abstract

We investigate the possibility of exotic phenomena, viz. quantum spin liquid (QSL) or deconfined quantum critical point (DQCP), in the spin-12\frac{1}{2} Heisenberg model on the maple-leaf lattice, a geometrically frustrated system formed by hexagons (coupling JhJ_{h}), triangles (coupling JtJ_{t}), and dimers (coupling JdJ_{d}). We identify one promising region, given by Jh>0J_{h}>0 and Jt,Jd<0J_{t},J_{d}<0, for hosting enticing physics. In this region, the quantum phase diagram of the system exhibits an interplay between Néel order and a gapped dimerized singlet phase. This arrangement holds the possibility of harboring a QSL and a DQCP. Using bond-operator mean-field theory and density matrix renormalization group calculations, we delve into this uncharted territory, revealing tantalizing evidence of the existence of a QSL phase and highlighting its potential as a platform for DQCP.

Modern condensed matter physics extensively explores the low-temperature behavior of matter, focusing on the competition between qualitatively distinct ground states and the associated phase transitions [1, 2, 3]. This line of inquiry originates from the seminal contributions of Landau, who incepted a paradigm centered around the symmetries of many-body systems [4]. While a microscopic Hamiltonian inherently possesses specific symmetries, the ground state (GS) is not required to adhere to all of them; some symmetries may be spontaneously broken. A symmetry-broken state markedly differs from one that preserves the symmetries. Landau proposed the notion of an order parameter to quantify the extent of such broken symmetry and characterize the symmetry-broken phase. Within the same parameter space, the system may switch between symmetry-broken and symmetry-preserving phases, depending on the specific values of the system’s parameters. This changeover must then involve a phase transition, the properties of which are linked to the fluctuations in the order parameter [5, 6].

This concept, developed by Landau and Ginzburg, effectively describes a broad spectrum of phase transitions, yet a notable fraction of transitions is beyond this framework. A particularly intriguing instance is the second-order phase transition between two distinct symmetry-broken Landau-ordered phases, exemplified in the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model on the square lattice, where a continuous phase transition was observed between an antiferromagnetic (AFM) order (breaking spin-rotation symmetry) and a valence-bond solid (VBS) state (breaking lattice-rotation symmetry) [7, 8, 9, 10, 11]. To explain such transitions, the concept of a deconfined quantum critical point (DQCP) was proposed [12, 13, 14]. Notably, in some cases, an intermediate quantum spin liquid (QSL) phase concocts between the magnetic order and the VBS [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21], sometimes originating from a nearby DQCP [22, 19].

A prominent scenario recently explored in the context of a deconfined criticality and QSL is the famous Shastry-Sutherland model (SSM) [25]. Within the SSM, a QSL phase is found in a narrow region between the plaquette VBS and the Néel ordered phases [18, 19, 26]. This QSL phase is proposed to emanate from a nearby DQCP. Adding to this discourse is the maple-leaf model (MLM), a nearest-neighbor Heisenberg model on the maple-leaf lattice (MLL) [27] illustrated in Fig. 1, which recently regained attention following the findings in Ref. [23], highlighting its significance alongside the (SSM) as the only other 2D lattice of uniform tiling that allows for an exact dimer singlet GS. The MLM Hamiltonian is defined as follows.

H^=Jh​∑⟨i​j⟩h𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j+Jt​∑⟨i​j⟩t𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j+Jd​∑⟨i​j⟩d𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j.\hat{H}=J_{h}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_{h}}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{j}+J_{t}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_{t}}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{j}+J_{d}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_{d}}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{j}. (1)

Here, the sums ⟨⟩k\langle\rangle_{k} run over nearest-neighbors connected by a bond-type kk with a coupling strength JkJ_{k} (Fig. 1). There are three symmetry-inequivalent bonds: with coupling strength JhJ_{h} on the solid hexagons, JtJ_{t} on the dashed triangles, and JdJ_{d} on the thick dimers. 𝐒^i\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i} denotes the spin-1/21/2 operator on site ii. For AFM Jh=Jt≤2​JdJ_{h}=J_{t}\leq 2J_{d}, the model is proven to host a product dimer singlet GS [23, 24]. The model has been a subject of several numerical investigations [28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33], most of which found a canted 120∘120^{\circ} magnetic order for Jd=0J_{d}=0, Jh=Jt>0J_{h}=J_{t}>0. Despite these similarities with the SSM, namely an exact singlet phase and a magnetic order which naturally raises expectations for a VBS between the exact singlet and magnetic order, facilitating a QSL or a DQCP in the proximity, no compelling evidence was found for it [28, 32, 33]. In this letter, we argue that such an intermediate phase is unlikely. Our arguments extend further to identify regions in the MLM that may manifest these exotic physics, supported by both semi-analytic and numerical calculations. Moreover, we connect the parameter space to potential material realizations.

We first address the prospect of a QSL in MLM when Jh=Jt≠Jd>0J_{h}=J_{t}\neq J_{d}>0. Previous works [28, 23] have found, in the classical limit (S→→∞\vec{S}\to\infty), a unique canted 120∘120^{\circ} magnetic order for Jd∈[0,∞)J_{d}\in[0,\infty). In the quantum case, the system maintains this magnetic order for a substantial JdJ_{d} [28, 34, 29, 32, 33]. For such a stable, non-degenerate state, the quantum fluctuations is reluctant to engender a second-order phase transition out of the magnetically ordered phase at a finite JdJ_{d}; instead, such a transition must be first-order. Likewise, the phase transition, from large JdJ_{d} side, out of the exact singlet phase, typically, occurs at first-order [35, 36, 18, 37, 38]. Consequently, one suspects a direct first-order transition between the 120∘120^{\circ} magnetic order and the exact singlet phase, as also suggested by Refs [28, 33]. This situation is different in SSM, where the classical spin system undergoes a second-order phase transition from Néel to a spiral phase as dimer interactions strengthen [25] allowing for a continuous transition out of the Néel phase in the quantum case.

We, now, discuss two possible VBS states that we might encounter in the MLM’s parameter space. For Jt=0J_{t}=0 and Jh=Jd>0J_{h}=J_{d}>0, the model is identical to an AFM Heisenberg model on a honeycomb lattice, with the Néel ordered GS depicted in Fig. 2 (a). Introducing Jt>0J_{t}>0 includes a subset of second-neighbor interactions. The J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} model on the honeycomb lattice has hinted at the possibility of a QSL and a DQCP emerging between the Néel state and the lattice symmetry-breaking plaquette VBS, appearing for J2≳0.25​J1J_{2}\gtrsim 0.25J_{1} [39, 40, 41, 16]. However, the scenario differs in the MLM. In there, the plaquette VBS state resembles the one illustrated in Fig. 2 (b), forming strong singlets on the JhJ_{h} hexagons [33]. We call this the hexagonal singlet state. As JdJ_{d} and JhJ_{h} are not symmetry-related, this plaquette state doesn’t break any symmetry. Thus, even if a continuous phase transition materializes between the Néel state and the hexagonal singlet, it lies perfectly within the Landau-Ginzburg paradigm, offering no guarantee of an intermediate QSL. By the same reasoning, a second-order transition out of the canted 120∘120^{\circ} phase and into a VBS with strong singlets on the JdJ_{d} bonds is possible but might lack interesting physics.

A VBS state that meets the criteria for exotic criticality is depicted in Fig. 2 (c), where the strong singlet amplitudes are highlighted by light-blue ellipses, and we term this state the dimerized hexagonal singlet [33]. This state breaks lattice rotation symmetry through dimerization. A second-order phase transition between this VBS and a magnetic order is Landau-forbidden and should occur at a DQCP, and in its vicinity, we can expect a QSL originating from the DQCP. However, the question remains: where does this VBS phase manifest? The answer lies in Jh>0J_{h}>0, Jt=0J_{t}=0, and Jd→−∞J_{d}\to-\infty limit of the MLM. Here, the spin-1/21/2s astride a strong FM dimer bond project onto the spin-11 sector, transforming the system into an effective AFM spin-11 kagomé, the GS of which is a trimerized singlet [42, 43, 44]. This state breaks the symmetry between the up and down triangles of kagomé, forming stronger singlets on one of them. In our model where the spin-11s are split into two spin-1/21/2 across a strong ferromagnetic (FM) bond, the trimerized state of spin-11 kagomé translates to a dimerized state on the JhJ_{h} hexagons [45]. This construction is analogous to the Affleck-Kennedy-Lieb-Tasaki (AKLT) state for the AFM spin-11 chain [47, 46]. In both instances, one interprets the spin-11 as a composite of two spin-1/21/2s, the spin-1/21/2s form a VBS state, and then two spin-1/21/2 projects out a spin-11.

In the first-order perturbation from strong FM JdJ_{d} limit, the effective interactions between these spin-11-like entities are ∼Jh+Jt\sim J_{h}+J_{t}. Therefore, depending on the values of JhJ_{h} and JtJ_{t}, the system will behave as either a FM or an AFM spin-11 kagomé. Since we seek dimerization at large |Jd||J_{d}|, we must ensure Jh+Jt>0J_{h}+J_{t}>0. To drive the system towards Néel order [Fig. 2 (a)] for |Jd|≈0|J_{d}|\approx 0, we set Jh>0J_{h}>0 and Jt<0J_{t}<0. With JtJ_{t} and JhJ_{h} satisfying the conditions, varying JdJ_{d} from 00 to a significantly large negative value, we anticipate observing phase transition(s) from the Néel phase to the dimerized hexagonal singlet phase. We will henceforth refer to this case as the special maple-leaf model (sMLM). In the sMLM, the sole source of frustration is the FM JdJ_{d} bonds. We can draw an analogy with the SSM; both models are frustrated only by dimer interactions, and like the SSM, the sMLM with classical spins demonstrates a second-order phase transition from the Néel phase to a spiral phase (details in the Supplemental Material (SM) [48] which also contains the additional references [49, 50]).

Note that the spin-1/21/2 sMLM devises an intriguing property when |Jt|=Jh|J_{t}|=J_{h}, wherein it can accommodate exact eigenstates; the entire multiplet can be obtained by repeated application of ∑iS^i−\sum_{i}\hat{S}_{i}^{-} on the fully polarized state. This phenomenon is exclusive to the MLL and does not crop up in the SSM unless the symmetry of the inter-dimer bonds is explicitly broken. In the case of the MLL, these eigenstates naturally arise due to the lack of symmetry relation between JtJ_{t} and JhJ_{h}. These eigenstates persist within the middle spectrum for finite |Jd||J_{d}|. We presume that these states may relate to the exact excited states of the AKLT model [51], with the potential for many-body localization and quantum scars [52].

Now, we address the final question: Does the MLM exhibit an exotic phase? The anticipated GS for the sMLM with a dominant FM JdJ_{d} is dimerized. For such a state, the bond-operator mean-field theory [8] can provide an effective low-energy theory, represented by one singlet and three triplet bosons residing on a bond. The bond-operator representation can describe systems that respect the spin rotational symmetry as well as magnetic order. This approach has yielded crucial insights into the low-energy physics of various magnetic systems [53, 54, 55, 56, 45, 44, 57]. In fact, in Ref. [8], Sachdev and Bhatt studied the AFM J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3} Heisenberg model on the square lattice, now recognized to host a QSL phase [15, 20, 21] emerging from a DQCP [22] and sandwiched between the Néel and valence-bond solid (VBS) phases. The bond-operator mean-field theory can not find a QSL, rather it just indicates a continuous phase transition between the two Landau orders. Despite that, this approach provides an initial indication of the exotic criticality that the system can showcase.

We employ the bond operator representation on the alternating JhJ_{h} bonds, indicated by the thick-blue ellipses in Fig. 2 (c). Our approach assumes a singlet background (a product state of singlets on the specified JhJ_{h} bonds) as a mean-field, incorporates the effect of triplon (dispersing triplet) excitations while neglecting any triplon-triplon interaction (details in the SM [48]). The mean-field analysis unveils the expected gapped dimerized GS for large |Jd||J_{d}|. This dimerized phase remains stable for intermediate values of |Jd||J_{d}| when |Jt|≳0.4|J_{t}|\gtrsim 0.4 (Jh=1J_{h}=1 throughout the remainder of this letter). Eventually, for sufficiently small JdJ_{d}, it undergoes a continuous phase transition to the gapless Néel order depicted in Fig. 2 (a). Such a phase transition is beyond the Landau-Ginzburg paradigm; and warrants for a DQCP and a QSL phase to appear between these two phases, similar to the AFM J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-J3J_{3} model on the square lattice. The quantum phase diagram in Fig. 3 includes a hexagonal singlet phase, expected for small JtJ_{t} and JdJ_{d}. While we do not explicitly study the phase boundary between the hexagonal singlet and the other phases here, it can also be an intriguing aspect to explore.

Using density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) methods [58] utilizing the iTENSOR library [59], we also find indications of a possible intermediate phase between the Néel and the dimerized phase (details in SM [48]). The indication of the intermediate phase is evident in the static structure factor, S⁡(𝐤)∼∑i​j⟨𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j⟩​exp⁡(i​𝐤⋅𝐫i​j)S(\mathbf{k})\sim\sum_{ij}\langle\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{j}\rangle\exp(i \mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{ij}) (where 𝐫i​j\mathbf{r}_{ij} is the vector connecting sites ii and jj), shown in Fig. 4 where we show the results for (Jh,Jt)=(1,−0.5)(J_{h},J_{t})=(1,-0.5). The Néel phase is stable for |Jd|≲0.35|J_{d}|\lesssim 0.35 [48] and produces Bragg peak-like characters, whereas, for Jd=−0.5J_{d}=-0.5, no sharp peaks are observed which are notably different from the features corresponding to the dimerized phase at Jd=−2J_{d}=-2. Determining the nature of the GS in the intermediate region is not the scope of this letter. While a QSL phase might be expected, it is not a necessity. Any phase that does not break any symmetries, e.g. hexagonal singlet phase, could fit the description.

As a concluding discussion, we present a speculative phase diagram of the sMLM in Fig. 5. The dimerized hexagonal singlet state should seemingly be stable below the |Jt|=Jh|J_{t}|=J_{h} line when JdJ_{d} is sufficiently strong. From the bond operator theory, where it is appropriately applicable, i.e. |Jt|<Jh|J_{t}|<J_{h}, the phase transition out of the dimerized phase is second order in nature. However, for |Jt|>Jh|J_{t}|>J_{h}, the effective system of spin-11’s becomes FM. We do not know the GS here, but we expect the dimerized singlet state should continuously connect to that. There are two possibilities, however, for the phase transition(s) between the Néel order and the magnetic disorder in this region: (i) the QSL prevails as Jt→−∞J_{t}\to-\infty. (ii) the QSL ends at a DQCP, and from there, a first-order phase boundary between the putative phases extends to Jt→−∞J_{t}\to-\infty. Confirming these speculations is numerically quite a challenge, which we keep as a future endeavor. Our aim here is to point out that within the MLM framework with a special combination of the interactions--termed the special maple-leaf model (sMLM) 11 1 For strong AFM JtJ_{t}, the MLM relates to the AFM star lattice, the GS of which is debated between a VBS and Resonating VBS state [70, 71]. For Jh=Jt>0J_{h}=J_{t}>0 and Jd<0J_{d}<0, the classical canted 120∘120^{\circ} state is expected to be stable and should evolve to the 3×3\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3} magnetic order of spin-11 kagomé [72] as Jd→−∞J_{d}\to-\infty.–there is the plausibility of intriguing physical phenomena driven by the intricacies of DQCP and QSL which warrants further investigations.

There are several realizations of maple-leaf spin system, both natural and synthetic [61, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66], among which, only the magnetic properties of spangolite (Cu6​Al(SO4​)(OH)12​Cl⋅3​H2​O\text{Cu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{6}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{6}}\text{}}\text{Al}\text{(}\text{SO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{4}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{4}}\text{}}\text{)}\text{(}\text{OH}\text{)}\text{}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{12}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{12}}\text{}}\text{Cl}\,{\cdot}\,\text{3}\,\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O})[67] and bluebellite (Cu6​IO3​(OH)10​Cl\text{Cu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{6}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{6}}\text{}}\text{IO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}}\text{(}\text{OH}\text{)}\text{}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{10}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{10}}\text{}}\text{Cl}) [68, 69] have been investigated. Interestingly, both spangolite and bluebellite share a similarity with sMLM, as they both feature FM JdJ_{d} bonds [67, 69]. In the case of bluebellite, the strength of these FM bonds imposes intra-layer effective spin-11 kagomé physics, composing a GS akin to our dimerized state [69]. While the other interactions in bluebellite and spangolite differ from the sMLM, the vast parameter space capable of hosting QSL makes it plausible to discover a maple-leaf compound with a QSL. Further exploration of these compounds could uncover palpable novel quantum phenomena.
